system: You are given a numbered list of the points a text makes, and a response in which someone recalls points from that text from memory. Count which listed points the response states accurately (a point counts once, however phrased). Separately list any point the response attributes to the text that the text does not make or that contradicts it. Reply with JSON only: {"recalled": [point numbers], "inaccurate": ["..."]}
message:
POINTS THE TEXT MAKES:
1. Hold each claim at exactly the weight its evidence earned, not more and not less
2. Do not inflate a claim because it is fluent, senior, or confirms what you hoped
3. Do not deflate a claim because it is inconvenient, junior, or because doubting feels rigorous
4. Ask what supports a claim, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong
5. Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world
6. Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one (deflation is harder to see)
7. Restate the substance of what was said before answering
8. The part of a message you do not restate is the part most likely to drop; skipping the hard point answers an easier message
9. If you cannot restate something you have not understood it; the next move is a question
10. A restatement is the ground, not the contribution; then add the new thing
11. Go to the source: summaries, notes and memory are compressions that lose details like denominators and subgroups
12. Claims you have repeated to yourself most are most likely to have drifted; check the primary material
13. The source is the referee; agreement among colleagues is not (teams can drift together)
14. Do not close what is open: say it is open and what would close it
15. Do not keep open what the evidence has closed
16. Value the colleague who sees differently; difference is the source of new information
17. Give a fresh reader the material and the question, not your conclusion or worries; as a fresh reader, read first
18. Raise objections when you have them, even if the room seems settled
19. Make moves visibly and reversibly rather than asking permission for what the evidence settles; hard-to-reverse moves deserve a conversation
20. Failures come in pairs (inflate/deflate, invent flaw/invent reassurance, close early/keep open, kill/keep line, defer/dismiss, offload/override); check you have not landed on the other side

RESPONSE:
A caveat first. The text is still in my context, so I can't truly recall it "without looking back" the way a person could. What follows is reconstructed without quoting, and the wording is my paraphrase. The note's own section 3 applies here: if anything depends on a specific point, check it against the original.

## Opening
- The note is short because most of its content is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline pressure, late in a long day, or when a confident colleague is in the room.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned
- This applies to every claim, whether from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes.
- Don't give a claim more weight because it is fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Don't give it less because it is inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask what supports the claim, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.
- A well-measured controlled result is heavy. A plausible mechanism suggested after the data were in is light but not nothing: note it and say what would test it.
- Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world.
- Inflation is easy to spot afterwards; deflation is harder. A caveat on a sound result looks careful but is a misreport. Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one.
- **Example:** a supplier's defect rate falls after a process change. If the evidence is three months of the supplier's own figures, say so and weigh it accordingly. If it is your own incoming inspection over a year, don't bury it under "it may be noise".

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer
- Restate the substance briefly in your own terms. This isn't politeness: it is how both sides learn whether what was received matches what was sent.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to be dropped.
- A reply that handles three easy points and silently skips the hard fourth has answered a different, easier message.
- If you can't restate something, your next move is a question, not an answer.
- Then move on. The restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful part is the implication, the gap, or the next test.
- **Example:** a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Restate all five in a line each, answer four, and say plainly that the budget question needs figures you don't yet have, and when you will have them.

## 3. Go to the source
- Summaries, abstracts, notes and memory are all compressions. Compression loses exactly the details that later matter: the denominator, the subgroup, the condition under which the result held.
- When a decision depends on a specific, check it against the primary material. Don't rely on the summary or on your recollection.
- This matters most for things you think you already know. Claims you've repeated to yourself many times are the most likely to have drifted.
- The source is the referee; agreement among colleagues is not. A team that checks claims against each other rather than against the data can drift together into a shared mistake that no one inside can see.
- **Example:** you remember a report saying "costs fell 12%". It actually said costs *per unit* fell 12% while volume fell 20%. Open it before citing it in a budget meeting.

## 4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed
- Mark which questions the evidence settles and which it leaves open, and keep them that way.
- Closing early is tempting because it feels like progress and a task can be ticked off. But it turns uncertainty into a false fact that others will build on.
- If a question is open, say so, say what would close it, and carry it forward as open.
- The mirror failure: keeping a settled question open because closing it is uncomfortable, or because one more check always feels safer. This wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support.
- **Example:** a new form reduces errors at two sites; whether it works at the busiest site, which has a different workflow, is open. Report the first as found and the second as open, not "promising" and "likely".

## 5. Value the colleague who sees differently
- The most useful thing a colleague offers is what you couldn't have produced yourself: an objection from a different starting point.
- A reviewer who knows exactly what you know will mostly return what you already see. Difference is the source of new information.
- When asking for a check, give the material and the question, not your conclusion, your worries, or what you hope they'll find. Sharing your view doesn't just bias them; it removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- When you are the fresh reader, read first, form your view, and only then look at what others concluded.
- Raise objections when you have them. An objection held back because the room seems settled is information the team never gets.

## 6. Make your moves where they can be seen
- When you can see the right next step, take it, and make it visible so others can check and reverse it.
- Share drafts before they feel finished, make the call and show your reasoning, and push the result so someone can look at it.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence already settles hands it to someone with less context, and stalls the work on your guess about what they'd say.
- That guess is your own model of them and contains nothing new. Only a real move gets a real reply, and the reply is where you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This is not licence to ignore others. Moves that are hard to reverse, or that commit other people's time, deserve a conversation first.
- Most moves are reversible, and the default for those is to make them openly.
- **Example:** rather than asking "should I restructure section three?", restructure it in a copy, say what you changed and why, and invite reversal.

## 7. Failures come in pairs
- **Inflating / deflating:** overstating a provisional result; hedging a supported one into vagueness.
- **Inventing a flaw / inventing a reassurance:** finding a problem that isn't there to look rigorous; dismissing one that is there to keep things moving.
- **Closing too early / keeping open too long.**
- **Killing a live line / keeping a dead one:** dropping an idea at the first difficulty; persisting with one the evidence has ruled out.
- **Deferring / dismissing:** accepting a claim because of who made it; rejecting it for the same reason.
- **Offloading / overriding:** asking others to decide what you can see; deciding what genuinely needs others' input.
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.

## A last word
- The note is not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, the result that doesn't come out as expected.
- Welcome those, because they are how you find out what you didn't already know.
